title: Some of These Days
origin: American vaudeville / early jazz standard by Shelton Brooks, published 1910 and carried into the hot-jazz repertoire, where its 32-bar chorus became a jam-session staple

pd.detail: Words and music by Shelton Brooks; first published 1910 by Will Rossiter, Chicago.
pd.sourceEdition: Chart of the 32-bar chorus changes as standardised in traditional-jazz practice, deriving from the 1910 Will Rossiter publication; no specific later arrangement or recording is transcribed.
pd.notes: Chart only: changes and form. No melody and no lyrics are encoded -- the head cannot be recalled reliably enough to write down, and the spec forbids reconstruction. The song is often written in cut time; per spec it is encoded as 4/4 at half the written tempo. One-chord-per-bar simplifications: where editions compress the final II7-V7 cadence into single bars, each dominant is given a full bar here, and passing diminished chords between IV and I are omitted in favour of the bar's primary chord. The 1910 verse strain is omitted because its changes are not certain; the famous 32-bar chorus is what the jazz repertoire plays.

notes: The 32-bar through-composed chorus, split into two 16-bar halves. Its signature move is opening on the VI7 (G7 in Bb) -- four full bars of it -- before falling to the ii minor, then a II7-V7 push to the mid-point cadence on the tonic. The second half tips onto the I7 toward the IV, returns home, then recapitulates the VI7-ii opening before the closing II7-V7-I. Bb is a common band key for this song, not a claim about the original publication key. Intro and outro are chord-only turnaround vamps, arrangement rather than composition. Chart only: no melody events anywhere by design.
